applicability: Declaring kernel signatures, scratch tensors, tiles, scalars, arrays, and tuple returns.
Choosing static versus `pl.dynamic` shapes for changing batch or sequence length.
Selecting row-major, transposed, or pre-fractal matmul operands and avoiding an unsupported layout annotation.
Writing a `@pl.jit` kernel whose tensor parameter is bare `pl.Tensor` and may need runtime-bound dimensions.
directions: Annotate static shapes as `pl.Tensor[[M, 128], pl.FP16]`; use `M = pl.dynamic('M')` only when the axis truly varies across launches.
Declare read-write parameters as `pl.InOut[pl.Tensor[...]]` and write-only parameters as `pl.Out[pl.Tensor[...]]`; do not write `pl.In[...]` in the local snapshot.
Insert explicit `pl.cast(x, target_type=..., mode=...)` wherever dtype width changes.

For a preformatted NZ weight, write `pl.Tensor[[N, K], pl.FP16, pl.NZ]` only when the static shape satisfies the fractal alignment constraints; otherwise load ordinary ND and let the compiler convert.
effects: Static shapes enable tiling, unrolling, and compile-time bounds but force specialization and recompilation when extents change.
Dynamic shapes reduce recompiles but hide loop bounds and may force chunking or dynamic addressing.
NZ weights save an online layout conversion and improve matmul feeding, but require exact physical storage and alignment.
`TensorView` makes strided windows explicit and safe but adds metadata the compiler and runtime must carry.
invariants: Static shapes are needed for many planning and tiling decisions; a dynamic axis cannot be used by orchestration-level work that requires a constant dimension.
`pl.NZ` requires a statically shaped, fractal-aligned tensor with a whole-byte dtype, `shape[-2] % 16 == 0`, and `shape[-1] % (256 / dtype_bits) == 0`; unsupported cases are rejected.
Packed 4-bit dtypes use logical nibble shapes in PyPTO IR. Physical byte size is `ceil(logical_elements / 2)`, not `logical_elements * get_byte()`. A 4-bit slice origin must be byte-aligned.

FP4 execution is backend-gated: Ascend950 supports `pl.FP4`, while local Ascend910B/A2A3 rejects 4-bit in-core execution. `INT4`, `UINT4`, and `HF4` remain storage-accounted but are not universal compute types.

Two separate `pl.dynamic('M')` calls denote different dimensions unless the same object is reused. For a bare `pl.Tensor`, `bind_dynamic(dim, M)` marks the runtime dimension; a fully shaped annotation is preferred.
`pl.TensorView` requires an explicit `layout=` whenever `stride`, `valid_shape`, or padding metadata is supplied. An MX `pl.load` must target `pl.Mem.Mat` explicitly.
principle: `pl.Tensor` lives in DDR, `pl.Tile` is an on-chip buffer, `pl.Scalar` is a register-width value, `pl.Array` is a core-local array, and `pl.Tuple` is an annotation for multi-value returns. Dtypes are explicit hardware formats; PyPTO has no implicit promotion, so every width change needs `pl.cast`. Shapes are static and checked at parse time. `pl.dynamic(name)` marks an axis whose extent is bound per launch; dynamic dimensions collapse to `None` in the JIT cache key, so one compiled program serves multiple extents, at the cost of compile-time shape knowledge. Reuse the same `DynVar` object when two annotations mean the same axis. Parameter direction is part of the signature. A bare `pl.Tensor[...]` is the default input direction; `pl.Out[...]` promises the kernel does not read prior contents and takes part in write-after-write ordering; `pl.InOut[...]` reads and writes and orders against everything touching the buffer. War anti-dependencies are not inferred; the dependency card covers that separately. The local API snapshot does not expose a standalone `pl.In` wrapper; use the bare annotation for inputs. Layout has two distinct ideas. `pl.ND` is ordinary row-major and never needs writing. `pl.NZ` asserts that the bytes in GM are already stored in PTO-native NZ fractal order, allowing a matmul weight load to skip online ND-to-NZ conversion; it is an assertion about existing bytes, not a request to transform them. `pl.Tensor[..., pl.DN]` is rejected, so derive a transposed view with `pl.transpose(x, -2, -1)` or pass `a_trans`/`b_trans` to `pl.matmul`. `pl.TensorView` makes strides, valid shape, and padding explicit for a window into a larger buffer. `pl.MX_A_ZZ` and `pl.MX_B_NN` tag GM scale tensors for MX operands on Ascend950; ordinary MX subviews are restricted.
questions: The exact 4-bit and MX layout support on future or non-local backends is documented conditionally; local 910B4 behavior should be established by compiling a concrete candidate program.
risks: Writing a byte count as an element count, especially for 4-bit buffers; the resulting under-allocation corrupts data past the intended elements.
Declaring a buffer `Out` when the kernel reads prior contents: the runtime may remove a real read dependency, producing an intermittent race rather than a type error.
Using the DN layout shorthand on a tensor annotation; it raises a parser type error.
Treating `pl.FP4` or other 4-bit types as available on local 910B4 because they appear in the type list; the local backend rejects them for in-core code.
summary: A PyPTO type says where a value lives, how wide its elements are, and how callers may touch it. Shapes are static by default; dynamic axes trade planning information for reuse. Parameter direction and layout are semantic inputs to dependency inference and matmul lowering, not documentation.
title: Types, Dynamic Shapes, Directions, and Layout Contracts
